Nvidia ($NVDA) shares now up over 4% in after-hours trading Tuesday, at a session high, after interim CEO Colette Kress raised the company’s revenue growth outlook for fiscal 2028 to 75% from 70% on the earnings call, according to Bloomberg. The stock had swung during the call, briefly turning negative before rallying. The results themselves are covered in my earlier post.

Kress said demand is “far exceeding supply” and pointed to both rising demand and more supply behind the higher outlook. She said Vera Rubin has already brought in about $20 billion of revenue, Nvidia remains confident in the 75% target despite new export rules announced Monday, and total CPU revenue should more than double next fiscal year.

On financing, Kress said Nvidia will be “disciplined and selective” in supporting neoclouds and is rigorously evaluating its investments, commitments and guarantees. She said guarantees begin only once a data center is ready to operate, and customers will need to show they have buyers lined up for the capacity.

Kress also said Nvidia is no longer shipping licensed Hopper products to China. Excluding the $2.4 billion of China shipments disclosed in the CFO commentary, third-quarter revenue would still have been about $113.4 billion, above the $112.6 billion buy-side whisper cited by ZeroHedge.

Board Chair Harvey Jones opened the call by saying the board doesn’t intend to reinstate Jensen Huang and would not take questions on his departure or the board’s investigation. The search for a permanent CEO includes internal and external candidates and “will be thorough,” he said.

"When we are looking at many of our different types of guarantees, much of the land power shell that has to be built and put together. Is it new? No. Did we change anything? No. What this is only saying is that we wanted to make sure that we have already communicated this, but we just wanted to make sure it was very clear as we had been receiving some of the questions on how that exactly worked."

John Schulman and Mark Chen on what research taste is, and how models might learn it:

John: "Research taste is about knowing which ideas are important in the long run, which ideas really catch on and end up going beyond whatever paper they first appear in, but being general and being composable with other ideas."

Mark: "There's taste, which is how you come up with the idea in the first place. The models are still not phenomenally good at taste. They go very deep into things like hyperparameter optimization, essentially tuning all the little knobs that you can tune."

John: "A lot of intuition just comes from personal experience doing research, but to get good at a certain research field, you also have to read a lot of the past work in that field, and you try to absorb the lessons from all this historical work."

"Companies will probably also just do RL from human feedback to collect data from researchers on which proposed ideas are good and which aren't. And that's kind of like absorbing whatever human intuitions the human researchers have developed and trying to bake that into the models."

🚨$NVDA cuts neocloud support plans down $1B q/q and adds tighter language around conditions; removes revenue share language from last quarter; adds new language that certain commitments "could be reduced or eliminated" if contingencies are not satisfactorily resolved. Bottom line: Total commitments grew 41% QoQ, driven almost entirely by a surge in 2028 supply/capacity commitments and long-dated data center leases, but the new contingency clause means a large portion is conditional on neoclouds securing external financing.

Also 10-Q to arrive "in coming weeks" seems like a delay.

Stablecoin holders are giving up about ~$12B a year in T-bill income . That income goes to the issuers.

There should be a switch into these products but the data doesn't show it happening. Since the August peak stablecoins are down $17B and tokenised money market funds are down $2B as well, so money is leaving crypto rather than rotating into yield.

Part of the reason is these funds sit underneath stablecoins as much as beside them. Ethena's USDtb is ~99% backed by BlackRock's BUIDL and its supply has fallen from $877M at the end of Jan to about $350M. When stablecoins shrink, the funds backing them shrink too.

They're also mostly parked. Turnover is under 1x a month, so the back and forth that makes them interesting for a corporate treasury is still more promise than practice.

Until access opens up they're mainly plumbing for stablecoin issuers & trading firms, not yet an alternative for the treasurer sitting on idle stablecoins.

In TradFi, money market funds are an $8T market. Onchain the yield-paying version is $16.6B, 0.2% of that, against $287B of stablecoins paying their holders nothing. Cash naturally drifts to where it earns the bill rate, so that ratio should be multiples higher. That it isn't reflects a market structure that hasn't matured yet (access, plumbing, issuer incentives), and once it does I think these funds end up in the trillions.
